utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. Yes, Mr. Harvey.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President, Your Honours. May I introduce Vesselina Pissarreva from Bulgaria who has been with my team since February and just passed all her exams yesterday at the University of the Applied Sciences in The Hague and we hope is on her way to do a masters in Maastricht. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Pack, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, we're going to look at paragraph 1 of your statement first. You were in May 1991 elected president of the SDS Capljina Municipal Board and party; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN KARADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. I don't remember the exact date, but that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: You were on the Serb National Council for Herzegovina until when?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN KARADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was on the Serb National Council of SAO Herzegovina, that's what it was called, until I came to Pale. When I was expelled from Capljina I came to Bileca. I spent some time there. And then in April 1992 I arrived at Pale.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: You were at Bileca until April 1992?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN KARADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: And in Pale thereafter throughout the war?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN KARADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, until the 31st December 1999.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: You weren't a member of the SDS Main Board, were you, during the war?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN KARADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was for a term.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: When were you appointed?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN KARADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember exactly when I was elected. Under the law that prevailed then for the election of members of the Main Board, they were elected from the grass root level and one provision in our Statute stipulated that appointments could be made by Dr. Radovan Karadzic, president of the party, and that's how I became a member of the Main Board.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: You weren't elected, were you, at the SDS party Assembly of July 1991, you weren't elected then as -- on to the Main Board; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN KARADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. You know, before me in Capljina the president of the municipal board was a lawyer called Vidoje Jacic, but he was withdrawn later as the legal advisor. Then I was elected. I don't know if he was a member of the Main Board. There's one thing I have to explain here, one thing that you should know. The Serbian Democratic Party was democratic and decentralised to the greatest degree so that presidents of local boards of the party, presidents of the municipal boards of the SDS, and even presidents of the regional boards were elected from the grass root level. They were not appointed by the president of the party. That is how I was elected, and only after I was elected did Dr. Radovan Karadzic find out that I was elected.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: You were appointed as advisor to the accused for political issues in July 1994; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN KARADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. As advisor in building up the authorities internally and for party issues.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: You knew the accused as a child since how old?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN KARADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Considering that I'm ten years his senior, I was born in 1935 and he was born in 1945, I know him from when he was born. He grew up in the same village as I. And if I need to say this, although I stated that in my statement, what I know about him is that he was an exemplary child, obedient, good, a very good student from the very beginning of primary school and into secondary school, in the pre-medical school, at the medical school, at the university who was one of the most prominent students, the most vocal advocate of student rights, and he was very involved in all aspects of the life of students at that time.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Are you distantly related to the accused, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN KARADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We are a very old family respecting old customs that no longer exist. And our genealogical tree is very broad. So the answer is yes, but I was not called here as a relative. I came here to tell the truth and for the sake of the oath I've given.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Transcript, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness said "with old charters," not "old customs." In line 19.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please continue, Ms. Pack. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: As political advisor, you were aware of the presidential archive in Pale which included an archive SDS documentation; right?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN KARADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was. But let me explain to make this clearer. I was an advisor and man number two in the party was the president of the Executive Board of the Serbian Democratic Party. As far as party issues were concerned, he was the closest to the president of the party followed by me. We also had the management of the Serbian Democratic Party and the director of the party. So these institutions, the management board headed by the director and the head of the Executive Board, held that documentation and that documentation was the principal document, the programme or platform of the party, and the code of conduct of members of the Serbian Democratic Party. Then various reports from the ground sent by local boards, Municipal Boards, regional boards, concerning all the problems on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, are you aware of efforts to remove and destroy documents from this archive, the SDS archive, in advance of inspections of the archive by ICTY investigators in 1998?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN KARADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, I'm not aware of that and nobody issued such an order.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Mr. President, could we go into private session?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we go back to private session.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Not necessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Go back to private session, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're back in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: You, Mr. Karadzic, knew a former advisor to the accused for political issues, you were not aware that important SDS documents were eliminated in this way, in 1998?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN KARADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: This was at a time in 1998 when the accused was a fugitive, evading an international arrest warrant issued by this Court. You're aware that that was the case at the time?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN KARADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please, at that time I was not an advisor to President Karadzic. President Karadzic had to, although it was not a condition of the Dayton Accords, he resigned to his post as president of the party and his functions ceased. We had a different president of the party at that time.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Let's move to July 1995. You were based then, along with other advisors, close to the president's office in Pale, in the same building, on the same floor?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN KARADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: And you describe in your statement having met with the accused on July the 15th, 1995. You also met him after the attack on and fall of Srebrenica on the 29th of July; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN KARADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I gave it a lot of thought when I received the questions for that meeting on the 15th of July, 1995, with the late Velibor Ostojic. That meeting lasted for about an hour. I didn't have the impression at all that President Karadzic had any information about what was going on in Srebrenica. We discussed completely different things. Ostojic was already on the cabinet, a minister and deputy prime minister. I know that economic issues were discussed, some problems in our companies that were only semi-operating, and we hadn't heard anything about Srebrenica. In answer to this question, I have to emphasise that the first news about Srebrenica as well as the earlier powerful propaganda spread by the Muslim media in sync with the foreign media about us as aggressors in our own country and our crimes, making up preposterous numbers so that the first news were that all the civilian population in Srebrenica had been killed, not that soldiers were killed in combat as they were trying to break out through our positions. And of course we always took such news, such reports with a lot of reservation. Because they said before that thousands of Muslims had been killed in cases where 350 were killed, that 70.000 Muslim women had been raped, that embryos of animals were implanted in Muslim women. And they never published denials of such news. These reports were just taken over by the foreign media. So we had absolutely no confidence in such reports unless they were confirmed by our own army --

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Okay. Pause a moment.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN KARADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- and our own sources. So we didn't discuss Srebrenica --

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Pause a moment, please. We'll deal with the international media in a moment --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I just correct one thing in the transcript?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Line 21 is completely incorrect. The witness said that Silajdzic after two months of the war said that 100.000 -- sorry, 200.000 and later 350.000 were killed and 80.000 Muslim women were raped. All this is missing. The rest is correct. I should like to ask the Professor to speak more slowly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And if we listen to the tapes, we can confirm this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I noticed the nodding, but do you confirm what Mr. Karadzic has said, Professor Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I confirm, and if I need to repeat it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please concentrate on answering the question. Yes, Ms. Pack, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Well, let's talk about numbers. You are aware now that by this time, by the time of your meetings with the accused in July 1995, you were aware that thousands, thousands of Bosnian Muslim men had been killed in organised executions; right?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN KARADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. This is a major controversy, and it's being terribly mystified. The first reports said that all civilians had been killed, women, children, old men. There was no reference to soldiers being killed, soldiers who were breaking through the positions of the Serb army. I am invoking a document, an agreement from Bratunac at the Fontana Hotel on the 17th of July, 1995, that was attended by representatives of Muslims, Serbs, and UNPROFOR. General Mladic was there on the Serb side, then the civilian commissioner in Srebrenica, Deronjic, and some other officers. There were three Muslims there and some Nesib Mandzic signed. And it is claimed that the organisation of the evacuation of Muslims was regulated, that an offer was made to the Muslim population to stay on in Srebrenica, and if they did not want to stay on, they could leave and that they could choose the route that they would take when they left and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, we are talking about the killing. I think you answered the question. You didn't know. We can continue, Ms. Pack.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: This document you're referring to dated 17 July, did you see it at the time, were you shown it at the time, in July 1995?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN KARADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have it in the book here, Srebrenica. If necessary, I can show it and there's the signature there. I mean, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: It's been admitted in this case as P03997.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN KARADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: This document, were you shown it in 1995, in July 1995?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN KARADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I found out about that document. I found out -- actually, not about the document but about the meeting. Our civilian commissioner Deronjic had let us know and that at this meeting everything had been agreed upon and that everything was fine. That I do know. And after that it arrived as a document, not into my hands but --

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: So you met with Deronjic, are you saying, in July 1995?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN KARADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, no. We did not meet --

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: When did you see this document --

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN KARADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- he let us know. I saw him later, later, after everything when the documents were being collected by this Mr. Ivanisevic who wrote this book along with a team of people around him. I did not see Deronjic because he was in Srebrenica and I was in Pale.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: So this is the one document that you've selected related to Srebrenica which you've selected to include in your witness statement. I want to ask you about the killings.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN KARADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: You've told us that there is a controversy around the killings, and my question to you is whether or not you now accept, after judgements before this Tribunal, that there were killed in organised executions thousands of Muslim men after the fall of Srebrenica by Bosnian Serb forces?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN KARADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not denying the fact that there had been executions; however, what I am denying or challenging are the figures that were never actually established. They went up and then they went down as everyone deemed necessary. Let me just explain, if I may, when it was that I first started doubting the actual number of the victims. At the first elections in 1996, President Karadzic sent me to Sarajevo to see Ambassador Frowick to have the votes counted that came in sacks from Europe to Rajlovac, and then we found out that in those sacks there were votes of those people who had been declared killed in Srebrenica. When I mentioned that to Ambassador Frowick, he reacted so violently. He said that I was wrong, although representatives of the Serbs had the right to count the votes together with the Muslims and Croats and I was supported by the representative of the HDZ too, and then I realised that he actually didn't want to have the matter clarified, whether there were people who had been declared killed, and if so, how many there were; and on the other hand, they voted from various European countries. May I repeat once again that I am not challenging that there had been executions, but I am challenging the figures and the way in which they were being established. Even as it was considered necessary to do it one way or the other. Of course I condemn this. Gentlemen, if you think that I do not feel compassion with victims, then I really have nothing else to say.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Can I have P4401 on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: This is in English, Mr. Karadzic. It's an example of one of the reports by the international media that was being written at the time. I'm going to read -- it's dated 25th of July, 1995, it's around the time of your meetings with Mr. -- Dr. Karadzic, and I'd like to read to you from the fourth paragraph. "In the days after Srebrenica fell, residents ..." and this is residents living in the Serbian town of Loznica on the Drina, "reported seeing 'truckloads' of men being brought to shallow pits dug on the other side of the riverbank and shot by Bosnian Serb soldiers. 'Dozens of people stood on a hill here and watched this,' said one Serb from the area who did not want to be identified. 'Last week I saw, with my own eyes, 50 men shot as they were forced to jump off the back of a truck into a pit.' "Around the same time, people reported seeing bloated corpses in the river. According to one resident of Loznica, at least 10 bodies were fetched from the Drina last week. People stopped fishing and swimming around this time, but the curious were undeterred ..." et cetera. Now, you heard stories at the time, in July, did you, stories from the international media of truckloads of men being shot right on the Drina, killings witnessed by Serbs in Serbia?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN KARADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can say the following. From my experience, foreign media completely sided with one side. They came to Bosnia and Herzegovina at the time totally instrumentalised. We did not know about that. We believed that they had come from democratic countries, that this was the democratic press, and unfortunately we were not prepared for responses of that kind. However, no one wanted to hear our story, no one wanted to hear our data. Such things, if we would try to deny this, first of all, we couldn't do it because we were not trusted. As far as I'm concerned, I did not know about this. I say, there were killings but there were also Serbs who, for money that was paid by foreign agencies, testified as they were asked to. I claim that and I know about that. I know a man who came from Belgrade to us, we received him naively, he was a Serb, and later on he stated whatever CNN asked him to state and so on. I repeat, a great poet of ours said: I was killed by a word too strong. Very often we were killed politically before decisions were taken by millions of words that were being spoken about us as if we were monsters. For example, they called our doctors Dr. Mengele [phoen], the embryo story, and so on. These are amazing things. I'm trying to be realistic. But gentlemen, I cannot and I never could accept all of the things that are being ascribed to us. Of course no one is without sin in this war, the Serbs included, but to accept so many insinuations and to play in an inhumane and un-Christian Godless manner with a number of persons who are dead, 5.000, 3.000, 7.000, I don't think that this is in the spirit of justice, and not only that, it's not in the spirit of God's truth.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: I want to move on to talk about one other matter which you deal with in your statement. You were in Bileca for how long?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN KARADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I worked as a professor, a teacher, in a school for about half a year, perhaps. I cannot remember exactly in view of my age. I worked at a school as a teacher at the same time I was an activist of the Serb Democratic Party.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: I just want to know how long you were in Bileca for?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN KARADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: So in the month of April 1992 -- I cannot remember, I tell you. Maybe I was there a half a year --

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Before April 1992 --

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN KARADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- I cannot, I cannot remember exactly --

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: You were aware --

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN KARADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, before. Before. When they expelled us from the banks of the Neretva river, when we were expelled by the Croats and Muslims, we, the Serb population. Then I came to Bileca, northern Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: And you tell us that in the first few years of the war Muslims from Bileca lived undisturbed in their houses, this was on the basis of your time there prior to your move to Pale in April 1992; right?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN KARADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Trebinje, in Bileca, Muslim were in the Serb army, in all fairness, at the front against the Croats. Perhaps they wouldn't have had it been a front line against the Muslims. They were there, whoever wanted to, others did not. They tilled the land, they cut wood. They lived a normal life. I as a teacher -- there were Muslims living, I taught Muslim --

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Okay. Wait a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN KARADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- children and we distributed aid that came from the Red Cross.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: You're aware that there were detention facilities in Bileca set up in 1992 in which Muslims were detained, yes?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Objection, Mr. President, irrelevant and outside the scope of the indictment unless it's related to this witness's credibility, which I don't see how it could be unless he participated in any of these things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Pack.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Well, he's testified that -- he's testified that Muslims lived undisturbed in their houses with their families in Bileca and Trebinje. So I'd like to just deal with this with one document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Please continue, Ms. Pack.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: So my question was: You were aware there were detention centres in 1992 in which Muslims were detained, right, in Bileca; yes?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN KARADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but let me explain. There was a big garrison there. There was a group of extremist leaders of the SDA who were suspects and who were brought in to this military camp. Nothing happened to them. Nobody fell victim in any way. They all got out. Please, it is correct, Muslims worked at the post office near Bileca and Plana, they also built houses, they worked elsewhere. I claim that. But a few of the leaders were brought in, leaders of the Party of Democratic Action, who in the view of the then leadership - I was not a member of that leadership - they were being observed and later on they were all released and no one fell victim in any way. This was not a camp.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: 65 ter 05616, very briefly I just want to deal with this one document. Thank you. I just want to take you to one page of this document. You can see the front page in B/C/S there. It's a report of a CSCE mission to inspect places of detention in Bosnia, report of a mission in August-September 1992. This is the conference on security and co-operation in Europe, their expert mission. I want to take you to page 32, please, of the English and to page 59 -- sorry, 27 of the B/C/S. Okay, there's a detention facility you can see identified there in Bileca at paragraph 11. It's not the military camp which you refer to, it's the student dormitory. "Djacki Dom," the student dormitory. And you can see there Muslim detainees, 74 of them, detaining authority, Serbian. You see that? That was inspected?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN KARADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: We can turn to page --

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN KARADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please --

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: -- 59 of the English and 39 of the B/C/S, please? This is but one example, it's all we have time for, but this is what the report writers state about this detention facility. "Former students' dormitory, 74 inmates, all but one are Muslims from the town ... 10 of them are over 60." It goes on further: "The food must be provided by relatives. The facility is overcrowded, there are reports about mistreatment, and one prisoner appeared severely injured. Ten prisoners are apparently held in a hospital after having been mistreated. A second place of detention was visited, but the police officer claimed that all prisoners had already left ..." You'd agree, wouldn't you, that there were detention facilities in which detainees -- Muslim detainees were mistreated by Bosnian Serbs in Bileca in 1992, yes?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN KARADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, please. Do you have information as to how many Muslim soldiers voluntarily joined the brigade, the Bileca brigade under the command of Obrad Vuckovic? They were there. First of all, people were taken to the barracks for interrogation and they were returned later. I know that. I know that at first they were taken there to provide statements and then that they were returned there, I did not know that. As for abuse, that is not correct; and that that was a camp, that is not correct. This was just brief detention where they were interrogated and released.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please, just to intervene. In the Serbian version it says all detainees had an identification card of the International Committee of the Red Cross, and in English it says most of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, I don't see much difference and then I note the English is the original one. Shall we continue? English also said "all prisoners."

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: You mentioned receiving questions about your meeting with the accused and --

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: I'm sorry, can I just ask to have those pages admitted into evidence, please? They would just be three pages I referred to, the front page and the two other pages.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, I continue to believe that this is irrelevant to his credibility or to any of the issues in this trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Pack, while the Chamber sees the need -- the relevance of the document as far as it relates to the credibility, I wonder whether we need to admit it given that all the relevant passages were read out and we already heard the witness's answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Well, I was -- my thinking was that the first page and these two pages, if they're admitted as a package it would be better able -- better facilitate a re-reading of the transcript and your judgement of the witness's response to these questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Then we'll receive it.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P6445, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, just very quickly, may I also say this is a disguised motion for reconsideration. The Court already ruled on the relevance when Mr. Robinson made the original objection. I wouldn't raise this matter, but this is a repeated ploy and I think it should stop.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't follow, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: The original objection was about the relevance. You ruled on it in order to allow Ms. Pack to ask the question. Then when it came -- when the issue was raised again, Mr. Robinson essentially asked the Court to reconsider its earlier ruling.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please, let's move on. We spend more time.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: You mentioned --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, it was admitted -- just a second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Pack, let's continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: You mentioned earlier in your testimony receiving questions about the meeting with Ostojic on the 15th of July, the meeting with the accused and Ostojic on the 15th of July. Those were part of questions from the accused's Defence team, were they?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN KARADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, probably, I received these questions. Lawyer Petronijevic [phoen] gave them to me.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: They were in writing, were they? Do you still have them?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN KARADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have them right here in writing, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: And you would provide the Prosecution with a copy, would you?

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Perhaps if --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we put it on the ELMO? Or would you like to see it first?

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Yes, please. I think they'll probably be in Serbian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, no, hand it over to Ms. Pack first.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Rather than putting it on the ELMO, because it is in Serbian, I think it would be preferable, Your Honour, if -- and perhaps we -- the Prosecution could retain it for the time being, take a copy, and then return it to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Professor Karadzic, do you have any difficulty with Ms. Pack's suggestion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't mind at all. I would only mind if it were abused in any way.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Will the Defence get a copy?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Are you done --

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: I have no further questions for this witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic, do you have any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very briefly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Professor, can you tell us whose garrison this was in Bileca?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN KARADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was a garrison of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Apart from the garrison was there a school of theirs over there?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN KARADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There used to be a school there for non-commissioned officers. Actually, there was a school for reserve officers for -- actually, first there was a school for non-commissioned officers and then a school for reserve officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Just one more question, until when were you in Pale, when did you leave Pale and where did you go?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN KARADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I left Pale on the 31st of December, 1999, I went to Podgorica.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic -- Professor Karadzic, while answering the question by Ms. Pack you said this, it's transcript page 16 from lines 1 to 5, I quote: "There were also Serbs who for money that was paid by foreign agencies testified as they were asked to. I claim that and I know about that." Do you remember having said so, Professor?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN KARADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't say that I knew about that. I said that it was common knowledge, there was suspicions, and it was known that there were people from Belgrade who for money worked for foreign media and they later became the so-called non-governmental organisations. They were doing this for money. I am very depressed about this, particularly since we did not have an opportunity to explain our position and to refute everything that had been attributed to us, although we didn't do it. And on top of that, our side of story was never believed. All the international members of the international community knew that Mr. Karadzic was willing to negotiate. There was an agreement with Izetbegovic and --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please slow down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. -- Professor Karadzic, my question was about those Serbs who testified for money. Could you be more specific as to who they are?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN KARADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot give you their names, but there are people and now I can tell you that there were heads of NGOs who worked for the international community at the time. One of them was Mrs. Pesic from Belgrade, Mrs. Pavicevic from Belgrade, the lawyer - what's his name? - those were the people based in Belgrade who were working for the US embassy in Belgrade, and whatever was asked of them they provided statements against and most probably they had their people on the ground of whom I know nothing. And earlier I was referring to Mrs. Borka Pavicevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: How do you know that, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN KARADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course I knew. They were publicly appearing on television in Serbia, saying that the Serbs in Bosnia were aggressors as if we had come from elsewhere. They did not want to acknowledge that we were involved in a defence war, they did not want to acknowledge crimes committed against them. For a time the wife of President Milosevic was also involved in this. She was saying some unfavourable things about us without checking them. Later on Djindjic's people from the democratic party of Serbia did the same, unfortunately. Now, if you hear such people saying such things, then you can only imagine what their agents on the ground did, what kind of services they provided, and I am embittered by that. Now, as for the names of people in Bosnia and Herzegovina, that is something I cannot do. But I know for certain that these things happened and that's a fact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. That concludes your evidence, Mr. Karadzic. Thank you for your coming to The Hague to give it. Now you are free to go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. May I just ask one question? Am I permitted to shake hands with President Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, sir. Have you completed the photocopying of the document?

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Not yet. Five minutes, so if the witness could be kept on stand-by just for a brief time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, you will receive the document which is now being copied through VW -- Victims and Witnesses Section in five minutes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And who is the next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, the next witness is General Radinovic, our expert. And I have a matter to raise with the Chamber before he's brought in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Mr. President. This concerns our witness Svetozar Andric, who is scheduled to testify on Friday. And I believe you are aware he has written to the Chamber requesting that counsel be assigned to him because he's concerned about his rights of self-incrimination as well as the proceeding in public session for some of the information that he's going to give. And since that will affect our schedule as to whether and if he's assigned counsel, he needs -- the counsel obviously needs time to meet with him and familiarise himself with his situation to give him advice. So I was hoping the Chamber could entertain that issue and act favourably upon it if possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you have anything to add with respect to his request to be assigned counsel?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. We strongly favour that and believe that an individual who is a suspect, at least in the State Court, ought to have his rights protected since testimony given in public at this Tribunal can be used against that witness. So we believe that in the case of General Andric, as we set forth in our motion for subpoena, there are documents which indicate that he has the status of suspect and could -- a suspect being defined in Rule 2 as a person concerning whom the Prosecutor possesses reliable information which tends to show the person may have committed a crime over which the Tribunal has jurisdiction. So although he can't be prosecuted by this Tribunal, the answers that he gives could possibly be used against him in proceedings in the Court of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and we think that he -- that his rights should be respected, and before giving that testimony he ought to have the advice of counsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What are the circumstances that would distinguish his case from the case of Mr. Garaplija?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: In Mr. Garaplija's case, I don't believe there was as much of a danger of self-incrimination as there is in this individual's case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Does the Prosecution wish to make an observation on this issue?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No, Mr. President, except to note that the final observation by Mr. Robinson was rather non-specific and conclusory, but other than that we leave it to the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And as regards his wish to testify in closed session or whatever, why was it not conveyed to the Defence in advance?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: I believe that he did convey that to us when he met with Mr. Sladojevic, that that was one of his requests. We don't believe that testimony in closed session or with any kind of pseudonym is warranted and we haven't made a motion to that effect. However, there may be times during his testimony when it would be wise to go into private session so that the testimony couldn't be used against him in another court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. The Chamber is seized of the accused's motion to sever Count 1. On this issue, the Chamber is minded to hold a hearing first thing on Tuesday next week. So before doing so, I wonder whether Prosecution can file his response by the end of this week on Friday?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That will be our objective, Mr. President. If for any reason that looks problematic, we'll let you know immediately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Let's bring in the next witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, General Radinovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Would you make the solemn declaration, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, please be seated and make yourself comfortable. Yes, Mr. Karadzic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, General Radinovic.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I have to ask you and even more keep reminding myself that we both make pauses between questions and answers and to speak slowly so that everything can be recorded in the transcript. General, can you please tell us the place and the time when you were born and your father's name for the record.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC
utterances.text: My father's name is Dusan. I was born in the village of Grbavci near Podgorica in Montenegro.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Even though we have your CV, could you kindly tell us briefly about -- your educational background?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC
utterances.text: I finished elementary and secondary school in my native area, that is to say elementary school in my village and secondary school in Podgorica. After that I finished military academy of the land army engineer corps in 19 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat the year.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I finished the command staff school in 1972 and school of defence in 1970. I --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please slow down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: General Radinovic, you are speaking too fast so that the interpreters were not able to catch up with your answer. Shall we begin from here. Mr. Karadzic asked you when you were born, but I don't think we heard that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't say that because I didn't hear that question. I was born on the 11th of September, 1939.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And could you tell us when you finished the military academy of the land army, engineer corps?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In 1959.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And could you repeat your answer from there, your career after your graduation from that academy, very slowly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] After that I enumerated the military schools that I finished. I finished the command staff academy in 1972 and the national defence school or the war school as it used to be called in 1978. In addition to the highest military schools, I also graduated from civilian schools. After the secondary school, I graduated from the faculty of political sciences, sociology or precisely political sociology, and I have a PhD in military science research.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us briefly, and slowly, something about your career, which positions you held, and the duties that you discharged?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC
utterances.text: After finishing the military academy for the land army, I discharged all the basic lower-level duties such as platoon commander, company commander, chief of engineer corps at the brigade level, and deputy commander of an engineers battalion. It all lasted until 1970 when I enrolled in the command staff academy. After I finished the command staff academy and the MA in the political sciences. I worked at the centre of sociological and psychological research of the Yugoslav People's Army, and after that I taught methodology of scientific research. After that I became a researcher at the centre for strategic studies for the General Staff, and in 1982 I became chief of the operations department at the operations administration of the General Staff that dealt with combat-readiness and development of land army. In 1986 I became the chair of the strategy department, the School of National Defence, and in 1990 I was the head of the institute of strategic research of the General Staff. In 1992 I became assistant minister for strategy of defence, and after that I retired in 1993 with the rank of lieutenant-general. Since 1996 I was an associate professor and from 1994 I had the position of an advisor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Can you just tell us if you received any commendations, awards, decorations; and if you did, which ones?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC
utterances.text: Of course I received commendations and citations and decorations, although I don't remember some of them. I do remember an award that I was given in 1984 for my scientific work in the JNA. This is called the 22nd December Award, which was the day of the Yugoslav People's Army, and that was an occasion for conferring these awards. In 1992 I received an award for publishing work in the paper of the JNA, for the paper entitled: "Changes in the Word and the Need to Upgrade the Defence Concept of the Country."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please have 1D21046 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, can you please look at these two pages and tell us whether this CV is consistent with the facts?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC
utterances.text: This is in English. I would prefer to have it in Serbian, it will make it easier for me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Very well. We'll find it after the break and show it to you. Let us continue. General, did you testify before this Tribunal; and if you did, in which cases?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I testified on several occasions before this Tribunal, notably in the Krstic case, Galic case, Ojdanic case, and at the very beginning I testified in the Foca/Kunarac case, but I testified only to the general circumstances, not about the empirical situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In domestic courts did you have any role whatsoever?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC
utterances.text: I appeared several times before the court -- State Court of Bosnia-Herzegovina as a military expert. That was in seven or eight cases relating to Vlasenica events, Kalinovik events, the case the deputy commander of the Zvornik Brigade and the commander of the military police of Zvornik Brigade, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us briefly in this particular case what did the Defence team ask of you and how did they set the terms of reference that you accepted as a basis for writing an expert report?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC
utterances.text: I was asked to provide an analysis of control authority of Dr. Radovan Karadzic in his capacity of the head of state, i.e., the commander of chief of the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What kind of material and which sources did you have available and what was it that you relied mostly upon?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC
utterances.text: I had numerous documents and material available. The most important ones that provided most credibility regarding sources was something that I called primary documents, that pertained to the documents in the real time, that is to say the contemporaneous documents. Those were operational documents produced by the conflicting parties such as commands, orders, situation maps, et cetera. I also had available the so-called secondary sources such as studies provided by other authors pertaining to the events and the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina. This is also important material because I mainly relied on the authors that I believed to be competent with regard to the specific subject and who enjoy a good reputation in the public. In addition to that, I had access to transcripts from some trials which were also pertinent and relevant for the subject. I also studied some expert reports provided by expert witnesses who testified here and that would be it. Of course, incorporated in all of this was certain expert knowledge that I have in this area and my ability to collect relevant while studying and fulfilling the terms of reference given to me by the Defence team.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, did you have sufficient insight into strategic documents of the warring parties and whose documents were the most readily accessible to you?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC
utterances.text: I had in my hand strategic documents of the Serbian side; in other words, it consisted of everything that could be relevant in order for me to answer some questions. Unfortunately, I did not have strategic documents of other warring parties. I did have tactical documents such as orders and commands that were helpful to a certain extent in reconstructing the conduct of the opposing side, but I didn't have strategic documents, such as documents issued by the Supreme Command, their supreme staffs, or other documents on the basis of which one could describe the conduct of the other side which was very much important in terms of providing response from the Serbian side and in my analysing the control authority of President Radovan Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellency, I'm looking at the clock. Is it the time for a break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. We'll have a break for half an hour and resume at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, sir, you submitted to the Defence your expert report; correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we call up in e-court 1D25181, to have it on the screen ready while we continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I hope the Trial Chamber will allow you to have your report before you in hard copy so that we can refer to a few paragraphs now and then. Is this the first page of your report?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In some paragraphs of this report from 40 through 43 you refer to certain expert reports done for the OTP. Could you tell us in a few words what is your main conclusion or objection to these reports? Did you agree with them; and if not, why not?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Are they not part of the paragraphs the Chamber ordered to be redacted?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Possibly. I have to look --

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm still not used to --

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, maybe I can be of assistance --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we ordered paragraph 39 to 46.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And you also ordered --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, there are several paragraphs.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: 39, yes, 39 -- you spoke -- exactly, it's exactly these.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. Then I withdraw the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, the Chamber has found that certain paragraphs in your report are not necessary and I ask you to keep that in mind and I will try to steer away from questions related to them.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC
utterances.text: I heard today in the witness room that the Chamber has done this, and of course I acknowledge it. But I was not able to check it and compare with my report, so I'm afraid to inadvertently make a mistake. If I refer to these paragraphs in my answer, I ask for your understanding in advance.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I believe the Trial Chamber will caution us. Could you tell us whether the Yugoslav doctrine and practice in the area of defence is similar to the same systems in other countries and whether one can understand the mechanism that starts operating in the defence system. What is similar and what is different?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC
utterances.text: Yugoslavia's defence system - and I'm now talking about the SFRY - was particular in every aspect compared to defence systems of other countries; namely, in the area of defence and security other countries relied primarily on the appropriate state institutions, the army, the police, security organs, et cetera, and other entities of course, whereas in the Yugoslav system defence was based on the so-called armed population. It is a deeply socialised system. When numerous entities were involved in its organisation and implementation beginning with citizens, working people, companies, sociopolitical communities, which means local communes, municipalities, regions, republics, up to the Federation, all that was included in an overarching defence effort. So practically the boundary between the citizen and the member of the armed forces, that is to say soldier, was erased. It was the constitutional right and obligation of every citizen to get involved in the defence effort without waiting for an order from above. This is very idiosyncratic and it is very difficult to compare it to other systems. Whether that was good or not is a different issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So conclusions based on analogies, would they be sufficient to describe to the Trial Chamber the peculiarities of the system?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC
utterances.text: I don't think they would. It would be very difficult to do by using analogy.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In that sense what did you conclude? What kind of war was it in Bosnia-Herzegovina? We're not talking now about the whole of Yugoslavia, we're talking about Bosnia-Herzegovina --

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC
utterances.text: Based on all --

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: It would be very helpful if Mr. Karadzic would always tell us to which paragraph he refers because I seem to recall that the Trial Chamber excluded a section where it was exactly about the character of the war and that it was a civil war and so on and so forth. I think that was also excluded. So it would be very helpful to know which paragraph is it relating to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Indeed. Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was just about to cite the testimony of another general from the United Nations who was a witness for the Prosecution and I wanted to ask General Radinovic about his conclusions in that respect, about the nature of the conflict. I don't think you excluded that because everything hangs upon that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll see. Please continue then, but is this part not dealt with in his expert report?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe it is. I wanted him to present it. I want during the direct examination to enable General Radinovic to present his report orally for the sake of the public and for a clear record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But it's easier for us to follow if we have the reference number to the paragraphs in his report.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I will try to find the references.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, we have heard General Razek from Egypt testify here, that's pages 5585 and 5589. In his evidence in the first part of his testimony he said that neighbourhoods waged war against other neighbourhoods, speaking mostly of Sarajevo. And on page 5589, he said that civilians fought civilians and they found themselves in the cross-fire between the warring parties. What would be your conclusion on this matter? Who was involved in the conflict and how did that reflect on command and control?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC
utterances.text: I came to the same conclusion --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before continuing. Yes, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, I see already a pattern emerging again. Before a question is asked, there is put something that a previous witness had said on this particular point. I think that is clearly leading.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Well, yes, indeed, he could have asked the nature of the war first and then asking his comment on other witness's evidence. But we heard the answer already. Do you have any observation, Mr. Robinson?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I think it depends on the question that's asked, if something is put to him for his comment without any suggestion that it should be agreed to or disagreed with, and I don't think it's leading, and I think it's a proper way to elicit a comment from an expert on evidence that's in the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In chapter 3 beginning with page 31 and onwards, you deal with the emergence of the Army of Republika Srpska, its structure, and the organisation and its system of command and control. Could you tell us whether you made an analysis and drew comparative conclusions as to how the armed forces of the warring parties came into being, on the basis of which doctrine, from which personnel, and what are their mutual connections?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC
utterances.text: All the three armies of the three warring parties came into being in a way from the basic concept of the defence system of the former Yugoslavia. All the three armies took over the legacy of the armed people concept, wherein the army draws its personnel from the locality where they live and operate. And thus, the war had a territorial character. All the three armies took over the doctrine of people's war from the former Yugoslavia, and that's where the similarities lie. The main command cadre came from the Yugoslav People's Army, educated in the military schools of our formerly common state. And because of that, even if they had wanted to, they could not distance themselves from the residual features of that army and that strategy. But there are other similarities as well. Both the Croat and the Muslim side in the war acquired their armies by establishing paramilitaries from the political parties, that is, the military wings of those political parties, military organisations came into being. On the Muslim side those were the Green Berets and the Patriotic League who started setting up much earlier than the dissolution of Bosnia-Herzegovina; and the Croat side did the same, through the Croatian Defence Council, that is to say the military wing of the Croatian ruling party HDZ. And of course, parts of the disintegrated Territorial Defence also joined these armies. The TO disintegrated as the state itself disintegrated. Only the Serb side did not establish its army by organising paramilitaries. Instead, it formed its army from the remnants of the JNA which was pulling out of Bosnia-Herzegovina and those who did not want to withdraw to pull out of Bosnia-Herzegovina stayed because they were born there and they wanted to stay there. They considered Bosnia their homeland and they thought it was their patriotic duty to remain in the ranks of the Army of Republika Srpska. In addition to them, there were members of the disintegrated TO which belonged to the Serb community. Also, all those armed groups that were set up in the process of self-organising of the people following the concept and the doctrine of All People's Defence that we referred to in previous questions. And the army came into being after the Assembly in Banja Luka passed a decision to establish the army, whereas the other sides just renamed their paramilitaries into armies.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General, sir. In Chapter 4 from page 37 onwards you deal with the strategic level of command and control in the Army of Republika Srpska, and that is primarily in view of the role of Radovan Karadzic, or rather, the civilian head of state and army. Can you tell us what your conclusion was there and what you base those conclusions on and whether this differs from some of the customary models and whether all of that was within the framework of the law or not?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC
utterances.text: Well, the answer could be both yes and no. First of all, there are three levels in the organisation of command and control, and that is customary in all armies: Strategic, operational, and tactical. The strategic level involves the head of state, the supreme commander, and the Main Staff of the army. The operational level is commands of corps and tactical level are brigades, regiments, these lower levels. As for the strategic level, there is an unusual, specific characteristic in view of all the armies that I studied, including the former Yugoslavia, namely in the decision on the establishment of the army on the 12th of May, 1992, at a session in Banja Luka, the Assembly appointed General Mladic as commander of the Main Staff. I highlight that, commander of the Main Staff, which is quite unusual. A staff has a chief, not a commander. It's not a command so that it would have a commander. In that way, it actually changed, disrupted, the basic role and the basic character of that organ, and that is professional. These are professional organs for the preparation of the military. So these are professional and staff activities, not command, so training, equipping, organising, arming, and staff in terms of planning its use in combat. However, by appointing a commander of the Main Staff, the Assembly from a substantive point of view disrupted the principle of singleness of command. So there was a dualism involved and that is in -- and that is opposed to principles of military command. Why that was done? Was it done because of the personality involved or did they want to emphasise that role or is this some kind of distrust vis-a-vis the political leadership? I really cannot say. I don't have a crystal ball. But that is what led to this low-level conflict between the two leaderships throughout the war and at times it even resulted in disobedience to the civilian head of the army and state, and there are documents to that effect. The Assembly, what they did, in your decision on the establishment of the military on the 16th of June, 1992, you repeated that and you authorised the commander of the Main Staff and the Main Staff for operational command. And in that way practically you conveyed the command and combat use of the army to the Main Staff. That can be done that way. The supreme commander is authorised to convey certain powers, but that should not be done fully because in that way he ties his own hands. When he's supposed to intervene, when he's supposed to ask for corrections, then he is not obeyed. So in that way actually the principle of singleness of command and subordination were violated. These are my observations, and of course we could discuss this at great length and in great detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What remained in the hands of the president after powers were delegated in terms of operative and tactical command? At what level and in what way could the head of state act?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC
utterances.text: The head of state kept important powers in terms of strategic command and control by defining military organisation, by defining strategy, then also dividing the theatre of war into areas of responsibility on the basis of that. The strategic grouping of the army in terms of various directions - colloquially, this is called warfare - that is to say, defining the basic principles of military strategy, determining the type of military organisation at its deployment and grouping, and also the basic strategic task of the army and also supervision over that, namely, that the army is used in a legitimate way in accordance with the defined principle for that strategy. The basic characteristics of the strategy were taken over from the strategy and doctrine of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. By way of an example can you tell us then when you said that -- that there is lack of compliance with the decisions of the supreme commander because of this dichotomy, can you tell us whether local cease-fires are part of strategic command and whether general cease-fires are part of strategic command? Did the army have the right to not implement certain things that were not strategic, following their own logic, if you will?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC
utterances.text: If I understand your question at all, which is rather general, at a tactical level the army does have the right to take measures that had not been ordered to it, but it goes without saying that, for example, a tactical position belongs to that; that is to say, moving, changing, deployment in order to have a better overview of the situation to avoid any kind of risks and so on. However, even at a local level an army is not supposed to violate a cease-fire if it had been signed at local level.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is the army duty-bound to carry out an order if that order threatens the safety and security of the unit involved and its members? Does the army have some possibility of deciding differently or asking for different orders?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC
utterances.text: The army has the possibility of reacting. If it is an order that does not involve a crime, then it is duty-bound to carry out that order. However, before that it is supposed to warn about the consequences of carrying out that order. However, if the officer insists on it being carried out, it will be carried out and the consequences will be there. However, the army is not allowed to carry out orders that would violate the laws and customs of war or that would involve a crime. It is duty-bound not to carry it out and to inform the order-issuing authority about that. And in spite of the existence of such an order, it is not supposed to carry out that kind of order.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In the documents that were made available to you, could you find any proof of officers of the Army of Republika Srpska being in a position to assess what is a violation of the laws and customs of war, to assess what can and what cannot be carried out?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC
utterances.text: They were trained to assess that. In principle, they could. Now, whether that was possible in each and every specific example, in a situation when fronts are mixed up and when positions are mixed up, it is a very difficult question and it is very hard to answer. I think that there were cases when they could not assess whether that was abided by or not, but in principle, yes, they could.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When you say "trained," where was it that they were trained to recognise that?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC
utterances.text: In military schools before the crisis, or rather, before the war in the former Yugoslavia, in all areas special training had been organised in this field that is called international humanitarian law. Seminars were held, manuals were printed and handed out even to each and every soldier. While the JNA was in Bosnia-Herzegovina, members of the JNA in Bosnia-Herzegovina had this distributed to them. Now, whether this was continued in all the other armies afterwards, I don't know, but I know that in the Army of Republika Srpska this was continued.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Analysing the role of the president of the republic, did you see for yourself, were you assured, that the president had issued the necessary documents in terms of respecting international humanitarian law and laws and customs of war, conventions?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I came across a countless number of orders of yours of that kind, and I think that there were even too many of them. Percentage-wise, most of the documents that you personally issued pertained to that subject matter, over 80 per cent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, the answer was already given, but I think the question was not proper because what the -- what Mr. Karadzic asked the witness to do is give a legal evaluation whether the -- Mr. Karadzic did all necessary. I think it is -- in an aspect it is leading and at the same time basically overstepping the borders of the witness expertise. It's for the Trial Chamber to decide whether Karadzic did everything necessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I didn't hear everything, but still he said that necessary documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I understood the combination of: Were you assured that the president has issued the necessary documents in terms of respecting international humanitarian laws and customs of war. I thought this -- this combination basically was what I was referring to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Well, given that witness has already answered, shall we continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, sir, a moment ago you mentioned a percentage, 80 per cent, of all the documents pertained to this subject matter of cautioning and -- well, behaviour in accordance with the law.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D9079, could I please have that called up in e-court. I believe that that's not it, 1D9079. Now it's right in the transcript. I don't think that we have a translation yet -- oh, we do. There is a translation, is there.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I object against the use of this document, and I can argue and tell you the reasons why I want to object even against the use of this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Would you like to discuss it in the presence of the witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: There is no reason to -- him not hearing us. The Prosecution opposes the use of this particular document for two reasons. First of all, it's the late notification of this very complex document. In its filing for Defence witnesses for July 2013, the Defence notified the Prosecution that it would only use the expert report of Witness Radinovic. Only yesterday afternoon the Defence notified the Prosecution that it would use a 13-page chart - and that is what the document is - listing 142 documents, if I counted it correctly, claiming that they belong in certain categories. The Defence thus violated point 2(F) of the Trial Chamber's order on the procedure of the conduct of trial of 8 October and it's the so-called 48-hours' rule. Usually the Prosecution helps and is supportive and accepts late disclosures and late notifications, but here we have to deal with a huge chart listing all sorts of documents, and therefore I will have to say the use of this document in court would be unfair to the Prosecution. That's my first point. My second point is the value and the purpose of the document. According to the same ruling, in the same paragraph, the Defence needs to first apply for leave to add a document not in its 65 ter exhibit list to be able to use it in e-court. And here is the question of relevance. As I said, the chart contains 142 documents of various alleged categories. The chart does not reflect how any of these documents relate to the report, such as whether the documents are mentioned in the report or whether they in any way relate to certain topics in the report. In fact, a quick review of the document yesterday evening and a comparison with the footnotes showed that only five of the documents listed are, in fact, cited in the report. There is also no way to establish from the description of the documents in their chart whether any relate to the excluded portions of the report. Furthermore, only 44 documents contained in the chart are, in fact, in evidence before this Court, so that the Trial Chamber and the Prosecution have no way to verify the accuracy of the categorisation of the documents listed in the chart. And as this categorisation of the documents is made in this chart, the chart may, in fact, be incorrect. Not -- and also I wish to mention that 47 of the documents are untranslated, so we have no way of checking what the document is really about. Finally, if the expert witness would now in this testimony draw any conclusions based on the chart, they would be unfounded and one would not be able to check the relevance. Therefore, the Prosecution disputes the relevance of the chart for the testimony and that is basically what I wanted to say. I do not think that at this point in time I also need to make further arguments related to tendering the document because that's a different topic and I'm not even sure whether the Defence wants to tender it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Who is going to respond?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can do it. Well, here it is. We believe that this classification that General Radinovic was kind enough to prepare and which we obtained during proofing would be helpful to the Chamber as a kind of tool per se. It is not a proof, but it is a kind of tool for the Chamber to understand my communication with the army which is the subject of this expert report. Therefore, I believe that the Chamber [as interpreted] themselves often did not abide by the dead-lines and we took a benevolent view of that. I don't think that it will be harmful to have this document presented to the Chamber. As for the other documents, we hope that during the trial through other testimonies or perhaps through bar table all these documents would be properly presented to the Chamber. If necessary, the General may come for additional cross-examination. I'm sure that he would oblige. We tolerated all the dead-lines that were missed by the Prosecution, not the Chamber. It was erroneously recorded in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The difficulty is this: If these cited documents, 147, had been cited and referenced in his expert report and this document is going to be used as a kind of aide-memoire, that would be okay. But if it was -- only five of them are referenced in his report and just thrown in in this way, it's another way of tendering another expert report.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But, Your Excellency, I think that the witnesses dealing with the description of the role of a head of state in command, and for that purpose he prepared a structure of written communications between the head of state and the army. In general terms he --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Sorry to interrupt you, but do you agree with Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff's observation that only five of these documents were indeed referred to in his expert report?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that there is much more and I believe that we are going to offer all these documents in due course, but I believe that there are many more than that. The table itself corroborates the conclusions reached by the expert about the nature of the role of the president of the republic in terms of command.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry, I have to correct myself. I thought you were asking me whether only five were admitted. More than that was admitted, more than 40, and our intention is to tender all of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I just wanted to confirm that we have checked the -- and we arrived with -- at the number of five documents that we found. And I said already before, 44 document are, in fact, before this Trial Chamber. But as the Presiding Judge correctly noted, this document is basically an amendment to the report that is in front of us. If he has now during the proofing reviewed additional documents not mentioned before and obviously not even seen by him before, if he has now reviewed additional materials, it's an addition -- this chart reflects an addendum to his report and that cannot be handed in less than 48 hours -- in fact, less than 24 hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
