utterances.text: Dr. Karadzic, what can you say about Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff's point, that 44 documents, 44 documents, contained in the chart are not in evidence before the Court -- are in evidence before the Court, just 44?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellency, during his work, the expert saw all these documents. So far either we or the Prosecution managed to tender 44 documents relating to my communication with the Main Staff. However, the expert - and that was our wish - should provide and paint a total picture of my role vis-a-vis the army and that is impossible to achieve without all the documents. And during the remaining part of the trial, we intend to tender each and every document that I sent to the army. So far we jointly - the Prosecution and our team - tendered into evidence 44 documents and there is about a hundred more of them that we intend to tender. What we were interested at this point was that within this general picture the expert should tell us how many orders to refrain from fighting for providing humanitarian aid, how many combat orders and other similar orders were issued which will be of assistance for the Trial Chamber to perceive what the role of the head of state was in the command structure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff, just hypothetically I'm asking you, in lieu of using this document in a lump-sum way, what would you say if the accused were to deal with each and every document separately, i.e., 147 documents?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, you yourself have ruled in the order on procedures already how additional documents and documents accompanying a report, how they should be dealt with. And I do recall that it is basically that not all accompanying documentation should be tendered but rather the report as such, and certain documents that are in addition should then be discussed in court. And I indeed think that this should be done here. If the -- if Mr. Karadzic wants to rely on some of the documents, and in particular on the categorisation of these documents, what they mean for command responsibility, they should be discussed during the cross-examination -- during the examination-in-chief here in court. That is what the Prosecution did with its own experts and it should be done here in the same way. And we are -- as I said, we are dealing with almost a hundred documents in addition to the ones that are already tendered and that are actually dealt with in the footnotes of the expert report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, the Chamber agrees with Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff's observation: It's tantamount to the amendment of or the addition to his expert report. In order to tender this document, you need to produce another separate expert report. So the Chamber will not allow you to use this document.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Then we can remove it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, in item 6 of Chapter 3 you speak about documents of strategic command with particular highlight on directives as command documents. Can you tell us briefly this part of your report and what it contains? I believe that it starts on page 50 or 52 in English.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For that purpose can we please have 1D25181.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] By referring to the manuals for command and control, what I did here was to highlight the types and groups of command documents are contained therein, in order to come to the topic of directives which are actually documents issued by the Supreme Command or the head of state, more precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you please tell us what is a directive in terms of its nature and its purpose?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC
utterances.text: That's a document of the most general nature in terms of command. It contained basic guide-lines, it identifies the objectives, and it defines the forces and the resources that should be used in its execution. However, a directive is not an executive document. Based on a directive, those who are responsible need to prepare operational documents that would implement the doctrine, that means draw up plans or orders, et cetera. If it is the Main Staff in question, then it has to issue its own directive. So it is the document of most general nature that does not have an executive power, only lays down some general guide-lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us if each and every directive is implemented in the course of period that was envisaged and what does it depend upon whether it's going to be implemented or not?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC
utterances.text: Since a directive covers a long period of time and since circumstances are changeable within such a period of time, in most cases the majority of things contained therein are not put into practice. So in that case, a directive has to be amended usually by operational documents such as command and orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If there was something that was included in a directive, intentionally or unintentionally, that would constitute a violation of international laws of war and other laws and conventions, what is the procedure relating to the implementation if such features are found in this general document?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC
utterances.text: The procedure applied is identical to the one when you asked me about the orders that constitute a crime. Anything contained in a directive which is in contravention of the provisions of the international laws of war, humanitarian law, and the rules of war must not be carried out. And in preparing operational documents, all of such features have to be discounted and dismissed. So nothing that is contrary to the adopted international rules can be implemented regardless of who issued the directive.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me how many directives I issued -- actually, how many of them I signed and what was your conclusion as to how they were generated?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, there was a total of nine directives that were issued. You yourself signed directives 6 and 7, that is to say two. The remaining directives were signed by the commander of the Main Staff. Therefore, when you look at a ratio of the total of the directives, one can see who had a decisive role in the operational command over the army, which means that in this instance the Main Staff overruled the role of the head of state. Now, how directives are generated? They are generated whenever there is the necessary infrastructure for their preparation, that means that they are generated at the Main Staff. As far as I know, you did not have proper staff around you capable of preparing directives. Any directive can show that because it demands professional knowledge and professional personnel. It requires knowledge that is called in general terms military science. That's how the organisation was set up. It would have been better if that were -- had not been the case, but the fact is that you did not have staff who were skilled enough to deal with these matters. As far as I know, the directives were being prepared at the Main Staff where they had enough personnel and enough information in order to deal with these matters. Now, how it came about that you signed some of them, I'm not able to say. From the substance of each of these directives, it is very easy to conclude, even for a layman, that they could not have been produced in your immediate surroundings, by your entourage.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The people who draft the directives before they are signed, they do this on the basis of what, which materials and whose materials?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC
utterances.text: In the methodology of developing directives, there are three methods. One is producing a directive through team-work, that is the complete method when there is enough time and enough knowledge of the situation and there is a long-term effort including numerous consultations with various departments. The second method is the shortened version. And the third one is without any consultation at all. It is produced then by the same organ who signs it. That happens very rarely. Most often directives are produced on the basis of proposals made by various organs, such as security, logistics, training, morale, information. In other words, commands of various corps make their own proposals for their own employment in the coming period. And then, there is an operative organ at the Main Staff who drafts the directive, putting all the elements in their right places with a certain amount of revision and editing, and then this operative organ submits it for signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Your word was here interpreted as "drafting." Is there any difference between what you meant and the word "draft"?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC
utterances.text: I said somebody composes, actually, the directive from various elements. It's not the same as "draft." The operative officer at the Main Staff cannot cover with equal knowledge all the areas involved, he cannot be completely versed with security and logistics and all the other departments. He can only put together contributions from various departments and from them make the draft directive.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In view of the latest technologies, can this draft be made by simple copy/paste of various proposals from different services?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC
utterances.text: Nowadays, yes. But at the time when these directives were made, I don't think that was possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When you said that in the operationalisation of general enactments, things that are prohibited are not implemented. Can you tell us what you concluded about the directives that I signed? Were there any changes in the treatment of these documents?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC
utterances.text: There is a great difference between Directive 7 and 7/1. 7/1 is the operationalisation of Directive 7. There are differences in the use of units in the scope of tasks given, the number of tasks and scope of tasks is considerably reduced in 7/1. And furthermore, Directive 7/1 does not contain the sentence that exists in number 7, so during operationalisation, it was noted that a prohibited act was involved so that was omitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In Chapter 4 there are three items where you deal with strategic goals of Republika Srpska and within that there is an analysis of the justification of strategic goals in the control authority over the army and the use of armed force in the achievement of these goals. What are your findings on this matter? What was the strategy? And then we will move to Chapter 5 which deals with military strategy.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC
utterances.text: In this section I dealt with the topic called "Strategic Goals of Republika Srpska." Strategic goals are covered in the record, that is, transcripts of the session in Banja Luka of 12 May 1992, the session where the decision was passed to form the army. At this gathering, you spoke about the strategic goals that Republika Srpska needs to achieve in that conflict that had begun in Bosnia-Herzegovina. I presented my understanding of your speech, what those objectives were, how they were formulated, how they were pursued, how they were achieved and whether they were achieved. I had to -- I would have now to speak about it in general terms unless you mention specific goals.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In paragraphs 144 and 146 you indicate that the war broke out in the middle of the negotiating process. You did not phrase it exactly the same way, but that's what it means. How did the activation of the armed component reflect on the negotiation process between the negotiators who thereby began warring parties, did it have an impact?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC
utterances.text: It had an important impact. In your strategic goals you spoke, even before the conflict, even before the war -- and, by the way, every party to these events had its own strategic goals and voiced them. As long as there is no war, it is implied that strategic goals are pursued through peaceful means. At that time when these goals are pursued by peaceful means and political means, political dialogue, debate, elections, some issues are completely irrelevant. For instance, the territorial issue is not of crucial importance; however, when war begins then the territorial issue comes to the fore. Why? Because if the war had already broken out, a necessary precondition is to ensure territorial integrity so that forces could manoeuvre from one part of the front line to another and be engaged in those places where they are the most necessary militarily. So when war breaks out, the territorial issue becomes the foremost issue. But as long as goals are pursued by peaceful political means, the territorial issue is irrelevant. And as far as I was able to see, in your speech and in all the interviews and various public appearances, you always emphasised that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, General, sir, we come to the issue of military strategy of the Army of Republika Srpska, the type of strategy that was used. Can you tell us about your findings and would you describe it, please, on the basis of all the documents and everything you know about the VRS. What was its choice of strategy and why?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC
utterances.text: I dealt with the issue in my report only because the formulation, the choice, and adoption of a certain strategy is the prerogative of the head of state, that is to say the supreme commander. Judging by all its characteristics, the strategy of the VRS was defensive, a defensive strategy formulated as such and operationalised in such a way as to only be able to defend the territory and the people of Republika Srpska. It is absolutely inadequate for any military option because the grouping of forces, their deployment, organisation, the assets in their possession were completely useless for the so-called strategic offensive. The Supreme Command did not have under its control appropriate military forces for manifesting its influence. It only had control over military corps, which is a typical feature of a defensive strategy. To use a figure of speech, I used to say: You cannot win a war with that strategy but you can defend what you set as your own strategic goals. So it was exclusively about defence, never offensive action. And I think it is not only unfounded but ridiculous to say that the VRS was an aggressive force because they had absolutely no resources to commit aggression -- I mean aggression in the military sense, not the legal sense.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In the light of what you just said, did you make any conclusions about the strategic goals, especially in terms of territory, of all the three warring parties in Bosnia-Herzegovina? What was the aspiration and the plan of each one of them?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC
utterances.text: The Serb and Croat sides to the conflict wanted to preserve and to defend what they considered as their own ethnic territory. It is debatable whether that was justified or not to consider their ethnic territory in that way, but that's what they believed and they defended what they believed to be their ethnic territory, whereas the Muslim side had as its own strategic goal to preserve the integral, the entire, Bosnia-Herzegovina, and that could not be done without defeating militarily the other two sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: How did that impact on the Muslim choice of military strategy?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC
utterances.text: It was by definition offensive, but in terms of means and resources, their strategy was too ambitious for the resources they had. So they kept trying to involve the foreign factor to wage war on their side which eventually happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: When you said that with a strategy like that no war can be won, can you tell us what would have been the outcome of such a war and what would be the role of the president of the republic in terms of victory, defeat, goals, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC
utterances.text: Many times in various transcripts of consultations, sessions, meetings, et cetera, I saw that it was not the goal of the Serb side to win but to defend itself own people and its own territory and its own identity, not to defeat the other side.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did the Army of Republika Srpska, in view of its defensive strategy, face the danger of failing to achieve these goals of losing?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The Muslim side pursued an offensive strategy but they didn't have enough strength and resources to achieve that. If it had have them, then it would have defeated Republika Srpska and the Serbian side would have lost.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What can you tell us about the choice of methods and forms of combat in Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC
utterances.text: In that way you were completely dissimilar to the military strategy of the JNA. The military strategy of the JNA in tactical terms was offensive, whereas in the VRS it was absolutely defensive. That means that the forces were deployed in one line with no depth or a very shallow depth, very easy to break through, and frontal armed combat, no manoeuvres, no infiltrations behind enemy lines, deep behind enemy lines, but it was all about defending lines, face-to-face. That is called the linear strategy, the soldier who lives where the front line is, who was born there, does not leave the line. That's why the war in Bosnia was mostly static with very few, very minor shifts of front lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd like to ask you to present warfare in Sarajevo to us, what you included in your report. Tell us, did you publish some books? I forgot to ask you about that at the very beginning. Within that framework, did you publish anything about Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did, a book about the Sarajevo theatre of war.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Are there any other publications of yours?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, the methods of warfare, the new world order, and politics of defence, possibilities of regional defence, causes and characteristics and consequences of the military aggression of NATO against the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. Also a countless number of articles, I never counted all these articles, I had them published in various periodicals. Also I edited many books and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you briefly present to the Trial Chamber the part of your report that has to do with Sarajevo. What was the theatre of Sarajevo? Who turned it into a theatre of war and what were the characteristics of that theatre?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC
utterances.text: I'm afraid it might be too extensive. When I say the Sarajevo theatre of war, I looked at the so-called narrower and broader aspects, all the way up to Bjelasnica and Igman, the wider one, and to the east all the way to Jahorina and then north to Visoko, then Nisici plateau, to the west Ilijas. So in the broadest sense, that would be the Sarajevo theatre. In a narrower sense, that is the urban area of Sarajevo along with Vogosca, Ilijas, Rajlovac, Ilidza, Dobrinja, all the way to Trebevic. So that's in the narrower sense, and the most narrow of all would be the urban area of Sarajevo between Mojmilo, Hum, Zuc, Olici and Bresce Brdo, so the so-called valley. That would be the narrowest sense. Now, what is important to note in this respect? Sarajevo was multiethnic --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I beg your pardon.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In e-court could we please have 2.2, 2.2, actions in the Sarajevo theatre.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I do apologise, General, please go on.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC
utterances.text: Since in Sarajevo there were Serbs and Muslims and Croats, of course, who were all living there, when the crisis broke out then these ethnic boundaries were simply taken. And then later ethnic armies came to these boundaries and that is how the Sarajevo theatre of war came into being; that is to say, throughout the crisis except for the movement to Otes, and that is the -- south of the urban area and that was in favour of the Serb side. And then on the north from Hum to Brijesce Brdo - that is to say Hum, Zuc, Brijesce Brdo, Orlic - to the advantage of the Muslim side and to the disadvantage of the Serb side, there were no movements. So those were the only movements. It was quite static. It was like a frozen conflict from a dynamic point of view. As for the Serb warring party, it was the units of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps that held the positions there on the Muslim side in Sarajevo. There were forces of the 1st Corps of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina that on the 18th of August when it was established had 15 brigades, as appointed by a decision of Mr. Izetbegovic, president of the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina, that is to say that is the first time this corps is mentioned, on the 18th of August. And there was the so-called Vikici Brigade of the Special Police with quite a few groups, armed groups that belonged to different individuals there. Some were also part of the criminal setting there which later became evident in various show-downs, Caco, Cele, doctor, some doctor. According to Muslim documents that are certainly reliable, the total number of people under arms in the urban part of Sarajevo was between 50- and 70.000, 50.000 and 70.000, that is. In such a small area, that is a very dense armed force. In such a small area, it would be very difficult to deploy so many soldiers without infringing upon civilian facilities and the civilian population.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What kind of structure accompanied these 50- to 70.000 soldiers in the inner city?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC
utterances.text: Units from corps, battalions, brigades, all the way to companies, so they all have to have their own logistics, their staffs, their equipment, their positions, that is to say where they were deployed. All of that had to be in town in the city itself, either in free areas in town or in buildings, schools, kindergartens, markets, market areas, administration buildings, that is to say without any restriction and without restraint. Civilian facilities were used en masse for military purposes, so the boundary between the civilian and the military was completed deleted.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In line 16, Brijesce Brdo, Hum, Zuc, and Orlic were moved to the disadvantage of the Muslims, but the witness said that these movements worked to the advantage of the Muslims.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC
utterances.text: No. These -- these areas fell into Muslim hands in December 1992.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I see the time. I leave it to you, Excellencies, to decide.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. We'll have a break for 45 minutes and resume at quarter past 1.00. --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.31 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, sir, can you tell us whether you established what the objectives were of the corps that were facing each other in the Sarajevo theatre of war; that is to say, the 1st Corps of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC
utterances.text: You mean in global terms?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Locally, Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC
utterances.text: The 1st Corps of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina had as its main objective to keep the entire city under its control and to deblockade the city; that is to say, to break through the front line with the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps and to link up with their forces in Igman and to reach the Romanija plateau. From there, the situation would be far more favourable in operational terms for military activities. The task, or rather, the objective of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps was to keep those forces under this blockade and not to allow them to break through to the free operational area in the Romanija plateau, and from there they would go to the Drina River valley and in that way the war would practically be lost for the Serbian side.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us how these elements affected the choice of strategy for both corps? Were the strategies identical or different; and if so, how did they differ?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC
utterances.text: Well, by definition, objectives are of decisive importance for choosing the strategy. The Sarajevo-Romanija Corps had its key objective to keep under blockade the forces of the 1st Corps and, by definition, it opted for a defensive concept, that is to say, they defended their lines. As opposed to that, the 1st Corps, in order to attain its global objective, that is to say to break through to the free operational area, they always opted for offensive activities. And now the fact that they did not have enough strength to do that is a different matter, but they always wanted to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. These strategies, were they justified from a military point of view and were they legal and legitimate?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC
utterances.text: From a military point of view, these strategies were legal and legitimate for both sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that the plan and the strategy of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps to keep the forces of the 1st Corps under blockade is quite legal and legitimate?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC
utterances.text: In accordance with principles of military doctrine, this is quite legal and legitimate, to blockade forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Who made up those two corps from a military point of view?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC
utterances.text: For the most part, it was local forces, or rather, the local population that had either been mobilised in the Territorial Defence or were in some military units from before. Basically, these were locals, and I think that most of them actually knew one another as a matter of fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did this affect the overall picture of warfare in terms of whether there were some professional forces there or forces that had arrived from elsewhere or ... ?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC
utterances.text: Well, of course it's different. We have already talked about the selection of activity. Had these been forces that had come from elsewhere, they certainly would have taken more radical action to change the front line. However, these were forces that were from this local area and they chose their way of behaviour accordingly. Since they came to these ethnic boundaries, the question was: Who had what perception? The 1st Corps certainly perceived this as all of Bosnia being their territory, whereas the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps had this other vision, that this was a separation line between ethnic territories.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. How would you then characterise the positions around Sarajevo, especially in view of this qualification, namely, that it's being called a siege?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC
utterances.text: From a military point of view, and that's the one that I'm only interested in practically, this is a blockade of military forces in the true sense of the word. But they cannot be blockaded outside an area. So if forces are blockaded, then the area has to be too. So this was a blockade of the forces of the 1st Corps, or rather, of the other side, those who were based in Sarajevo; it wasn't only the 1st Corps, there was also the special brigade of the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: According to the documents that you obtained, did you reach a conclusion as to whether the Muslim side had an alternative to this blockade and deblockade? Could the situation be resolved in a different way in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, in a completely different way. First of all, there didn't have to be a conflict in the first place. Government could have been organised on the basis of majority rule, where ethnic communities were a majority. In particular municipalities, the government could have been organised accordingly. And then also an open city could have been declared; that is to say, demilitarisation and UN mechanisms could have run the city and that way there wouldn't have been any conflicts and there wouldn't have been any casualties, not even military casualties let alone civilian ones.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know what my position was in terms of demilitarisation and allowing the UN to run Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC
utterances.text: You advocated demilitarisation, the demilitarisation of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I would like to ask you, in view of what is claimed in the indictment, namely, that Sarajevo was under siege and that the population was being terrorised and that that was the objective, did you find anywhere in documents or reports, did you find any proof for that kind of allegation?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC
utterances.text: For blockade of military forces, yes, because I wasn't actually counting so I don't want to exaggerate, but in most military documents, coming from both sides that is, the forces of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps pointed out this task of preventing deblockade, that is to say preventing the departure of military forces from Sarajevo. In the documents of the units of the 1st Corps of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, almost always there was a reference to the need to deblockade Sarajevo, to leave the city, and to link up with the forces that were attacking from Central Bosnia, or rather, at Mount Igman.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The Sarajevo-Romanija Corps and the forces in the city itself and the forces on the outside, on the external line, what was actually the situation in terms of numbers between these two armed forces?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC
utterances.text: The Sarajevo-Romanija Corps had a maximum of 22.000 people, between 18- and 22.000, so say roughly around 20.000. And the 1st Corps of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina had over 50.000. So it was at least 2:1 in favour of the forces of the 1st Corps of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. If we were to take other factors into account too, like combat equipment and so on, then there would be a balance. It would not be to the detriment of the Serb side to such a degree, but at any rate they outnumbered the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps and that was the main handicap for the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, that the situation was such in Sarajevo and vis-a-vis the 1st Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And what is the situation if taking into account that the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps was also fighting against the 2nd, 3rd, and 4th Corps on the other side externally?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC
utterances.text: It is far more unfavourable when you take that into account because the thrust of their activity was towards the outside.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you find any proof that the Serbian army, i.e., the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, attacked the city in order to terrorise civilians?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't find any such proof in any of the documents. It does not necessarily have to be explicitly articulated, but having studied the entire context of the situation I did not come to that conclusion. Now, what was that indication that led me to this conclusion? There were long periods without any activity. Further on there were cease-fires that lasted for a certain period of time which were not characterised by any activities. Had it been the case of terrorised civilians, I don't think that there would be an observance of such long periods without any activities. There's another fact that can speak in favour of my claim that this was not a matter of terrorising the civilian population. I don't know how many places of worship are in Sarajevo, but I'm sure there are quite a few of them. The simplest way to terrorise civilians is to do that while they are attending these places of worship. As far as I know, there were no such incidents which convinced me that this was not the issue of terrorising civilians but rather the issue of casualties that were caused by various --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please move closer to the microphone. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I already sensed the speeding up of both interlocutors, and please put a pause between the questions and answers. And, General Radinovic, if you could come closer to the microphone. Yes. Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let me just see if you have finished your answer. You said "caused by various circumstances." Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Have you established that there were periods when the Serbian side opened fire unilaterally, when there was no exchange of fire but rather unilateral fire coming from the Serbian side with the aim of obtaining any goal, in particular the terrorising of civilians?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC
utterances.text: No, I haven't come across such situations.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So from which parts of Sarajevo did fire come from and where was it aimed?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC
utterances.text: The fire was coming from the centre of the city and fire was returned from the edges of the city.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You said that Sarajevo was rather densely militarised. In your opinion, in view of the General Staff and then the staff of the 1st Corps, the staff of the 12th Division, and staffs of these 15 brigades, battalions, and companies, how many stationary legitimate military targets were in the city of Sarajevo, and I'm talking about military targets?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC
utterances.text: I made some kind of analysis and some kind of calculations; however, these kind of calculations can never be accurate. There is always a margin of error. If you take that an average legitimate military target according to the doctrine would be a squad occupying a certain position - but a legitimate target can also be a piece of an artillery or a command post; for example, communications stations and posts - so if I put this -- all this together, I reached a figure that there were 2.200 legitimate military targets in the city of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you come across any document that I sent to the army, that is to say the Main Staff or the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, ordering an aggressive conduct of the army against the city of Sarajevo or containing any unlawful elements or ordering unlawful conduct and the use of unnecessary force?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC
utterances.text: I haven't come across any such document. On the contrary, I saw documents in which you ordered them to demonstrate restraint and ban on attacking the airport, UNPROFOR, and the city itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Here we had an opportunity to see several reports by UNMOs. Did you have an opportunity to become familiarised with these kind of reports?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: According to what you have reviewed, can you tell us if the UNMOs in terms of their numbers and in terms of having five observation posts, 11 of them were with Muslims in the city, were they able to provide accurate reports in terms of whether fire was justified or lawful?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC
utterances.text: I am fully convinced and I wrote this down that the UNMOs with such a low number of observation posts were not able to establish the accurate situation, especially since they didn't know where certain elements of the combat disposition of the 1st Corps were located.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We had an opportunity to see that foreign journalists decided that fire was coming from the Serbs because it was coming from the surrounding hills. Can you tell us what was the disposition of forces with regard to the dominant features around Sarajevo facing the inner circle?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC
utterances.text: The closest features are Mojmilo; Brijesce Brdo; Orlic; Zuc; Hum; Colina Kapa, Velika and Mala. So these are the features that make a circle around or a ring around the city proper. All of these features, with the exception of Trebevic which is above Colina Kapa and Radare [phoen] which is to the north of Sarajevo were held by the 1st Corps of the BH Army. So it is absolutely untrue that the forces of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps held these elevated points above the city and used them to open uncontrolled fire at the city. For example, Igman was held exclusively by the 1st Corps of BH Army, which controlled virtually and effectively the city itself; and from Zuc you could also control Mojmilo. And all these positions were held by the BH army.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When you spoke about stationary military targets, was the manoeuvring space, the room for rotations and supplies, a legitimate military target?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, they are. All military movements, including convoys bringing supplies, the reinforcements, the personnel who's going to take over the lines, et cetera, the command, all of these are legitimate military targets.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So what is necessary for a conclusion that fire was random and undiscriminating? What is necessary to conclude that a shell, for instance, was unjustified?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC
utterances.text: First of all, there should be no military forces at the place where the shell impacted. It would be necessary for there to have been no military movements in that area, to make it a legitimate target. It would be necessary to carry out an expert investigation on site to determine who fired, what he was aiming at, et cetera. We don't have that, unfortunately. We only have evidence of fire, and when we registered that in a certain locality where the shell impacted there were no military forces, but we don't know about the period before that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In addition to military personnel, was it possible to also remove firing positions so that at one moment they are there and at another there are none? Was that a tactic the 1st Corps of the BH Army used in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC
utterances.text: The 1st Corps of the BH Army in Sarajevo used all the tactics that is normally employed in the so-called urban warfare, that means that manoeuvring was very intense inside the town. They would mount weapons on a trailer or a cart or a car, fire, and move it, so the target is lost and the opposite side returns fire. And then it seems as if they were firing at random, at no particular target.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, since a few minutes I start wondering whether the witness is testifying here as an expert based on documents or whether he's testifying here now as an eye-witness, as an investigator looking at certain incidents in detail. Now, I'm really surprised and I was wondering whether what he is now talking about with Mr. Karadzic is, in fact, his expertise, in particular in light of paragraph 20 of his expert report, where he explicitly says that those kind of details are a matter of a expert report of a different kind. It would be separate reports that would deal with these kind of incidents. I get the impression that we are now leaving the expert report but going into a field of eye-witness knowledge or hearsay knowledge even. I don't know whether it's still document related and expert view evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, would you like to respond to this?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Gladly. I believe that Dr. Radinovic has dealt with the features of the Sarajevo theatre of war in his report. I cannot give you the reference to a particular chapter, but for instance 306, paragraph 306 speaks about Zuc, Grdonj, Velika, Colina Kapa, Mala Colina Kapa, various hills, Grdonj, then in paragraph 36 he speaks about sniping which I haven't reached yet. I believe in one paragraph he also speaks about undiscriminating random fire and disproportionate responses. So the Sarajevo theatre of war is the subject of these paragraphs. Beginning with page 105, 106, and onwards.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Maybe I can be more specific. He said, for instance, to establish -- I'm looking here at page 74, line 7 started when he starts to speak about how to establish a legitimate target he says: "It would be necessary to carry out an expert investigation on site to determine who fired, what he was aiming at," et cetera. And he says: "We don't have that, unfortunately. We only have evidence of fire, and when we registered that in a certain locality where the shell impacted there were no military forces, but we don't know about the period before that." I mean, that is eye-witness evidence. It's not something that arrives from the expert -- from the report that he did. And he himself said in paragraph 20 that this would be a different report. And there is also -- there is also this reference: "They would mount weapons on a trailer or a cart or a car, fire and move it so the target is lost and the opposite side returns fire." That's again more what an eye-witness on the ground would be able to testify to and we did have these witnesses, in fact, in court.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I wouldn't agree. Paragraphs 290 and onwards deal with exchanges of fire. They deal with -- 298 speaks about observers, 299 about observers and their reports. The monitoring reports underlie a great part of the indictment. The General was not an eye-witness. I just asked him what he established on the basis of documents. I always put questions based on documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But answering such answers as cited by Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff without referencing any document sounds as if he were testifying as part of investigation -- as a capacity of investigator or eye-witness, et cetera. I tend to agree with Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff's observation. Shall we continue, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, sir, in paragraph 300 you wrote about the proportionality of fire from mortars and material. Could we see in e-court one document that you cite in footnote 190, that's 1D9092. While we wait for that, could you tell us what is the foundation for your conclusions about proportional or unproportional fire? Is it the number of shells on either side or the attainment of a target or something else?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC
utterances.text: In the military doctrine, at least as far as I was able to study it, and I also created it in part, there are no empiric criteria based on which we could determine whether fire was proportionate or not. So whenever somebody claims that fire was disproportionate, it is a judgement call, it is a value judgement. It is not objective. There is no criterion that would determine or prescribe how many shells need to be fired in order for fire to be disproportionate. Why? Because one cannot envisage or foresee all the circumstances on the front line that would factor into such a decision. So what remains is just a value judgement, that a target should not be subjected to unnecessary devastation but to respond in such a way as to repel the threat. The only thing that exists and that works for mortar 92- and 120-millimetres, there are a certain number of shells that need to be fired in order to neutralise the target in a certain percentage. For 82-millimetre mortars, that percentage is between 15 to 25 per cent or 50 per cent neutralisation. There is a certain number of shells linked to that. For the 120-millimetre mortar, there is a prescribed number of shells necessary to achieve 50 per cent neutralisation of the target. But even that should be taken with a grain of salt because it depends on the condition of the target on what terrain it lies. There are norms that follow from experience and from regulations, but I'm not sure that this would be the correct experimental result that would apply to all possible circumstances on the front line, on the battleground. When we make a negative call that fire was disproportionate, we are not dealing with exact facts but with value judgements.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us, what is this document before us?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC
utterances.text: That is the rule for the 82-millimetre mortar.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What does it stipulate?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC
utterances.text: It stipulates how that weapon should be used, how it should be handled, operated, what kind of fire is achieved, how it is charged, the body of knowledge necessary to use the weapon efficiently.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we see page 268, paragraph 432. In e-court that would be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We have it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Oh, we have it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Page 11.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what this paragraph is about?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC
utterances.text: You mean 432? Neutralising personnel and firing assets outside of cover using a mortar squad and platoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So what is considered to proportionate? How many shells are allowed to be fired? How many is it possible to fire? First of all, would a mortar be used for that purpose in urban areas, to neutralise personnel and their own mortars, for instance?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's what it's used for and it's a very good weapon to use for that purpose because it has a downward trajectory, so even targets covered by tall buildings could be hit.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And what does the next paragraph deal with?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC
utterances.text: Neutralising personnel and weapons behind cover requires --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It is combined.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. It talks about systematic fire, that means sustained fire over a period of time that is necessary to destroy a target. That's the method. And fire strikes are a concentration of fire at certain intervals necessary to destroy the target.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is with the aim of destruction. And what about sustained fire, what is its purpose?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC
utterances.text: Its purpose is only to prevent fire against one's own forces. It keeps the weapon or personnel in fear, disabling them from opening fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And how many shells are prescribed? Is there a prescribed number of shells to shut up that weapon, so to speak?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC
utterances.text: There is no prescribed number, but it's legitimate activity on the condition, of course, that it doesn't threaten civilians, that civilians are relocated.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Knowing from the documents the circumstances that prevailed in Sarajevo, what was the responsibility of the warring parties for each other's civilians and did there exist responsibility to one's own civilians and what kind?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC
utterances.text: There was responsibility to civilians on all sides. A military commander is duty-bound to evacuate civilian population from the zone of combat, where they could be in physical danger. So they have to remove civilians. As for the civilians of the opposite side, the military commander must not make them a military target if the disposition of the enemy forces allows him to do so. That means he may not target civilians that are physically separated from enemy forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What would be the role of the enemy commander, that is to say the command of enemy forces, relative to their own civilians? For instance, the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps has certain obligations. Are they unconditional or is it also the obligation of the other side to enable civilians to be spared?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC
utterances.text: The military commander has the duty to make it impossible to abuse or misuse the civilian population for military purposes. That means that civilian buildings may not be used for military purposes if they want them to be excluded, not to be a military target. However, if a civilian building is used to house a firing position, armed personnel, et cetera, from that moment on that building becomes a legitimate military target and they cannot reckon with being spared from fire from the other side. So each commander has the obligation to refrain from using civilian buildings for military purposes if that is possible. The question is: Was it possible under the given circumstances?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We've heard General Dzambasovic, I'm sorry I'm not able to produce a reference, the page number, saying that the -- there was so little room that they could not move their weapons and assets far away enough from civilians. What would you say?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC
utterances.text: I believe him. I would also say it was impossible. With such a concentration of military forces in such a small space, it was impossible not to use civilian buildings for military purposes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I tender this document to be MFI'd pending translation? It's also mentioned in the report. That would, in fact, be paragraphs from 415 through 437. There's reference in footnote 190.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We only saw page 268 and the next page in terms of paragraph -- paragraphs 432, 433.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Your Excellency, it is possible for us to look at all of it, but these few paragraphs are useful for the Chamber. We don't need to go through each and every one of them because they all speak about similar subjects only under different circumstances, and we also have tables with the usual bursts of fire. However, if you wish me to do so, I can go through each and every item, but I think that once it is translated it is going to be of assistance to the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: The only problem that I see is that I can't read it. That's a problem. I do not really see how these other pages are related to the one that we have talked about, for instance, the tables. Are these firing tables and how many shells need to be fired to neutralise a target? These kind of things, then I would say it's related and we would -- should admit it -- at least marked for identification. But I cannot really say that. Perhaps Mr. Karadzic should address a few more paragraphs and see how it is related.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff. Following our practice we'll admit e-court pages 1 to 3 and 11. We'll mark it for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As MFI D3862.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please have page 262.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, under 417, the bold section speaks about insufficient accuracy for group firing and the effects on the use of mortars. Can you tell us, is that also a factor that affects the number of mortars?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC
utterances.text: Of course it does. First of all, it depends on the number of approved ammunition because for every activity a certain amount of ammunition has to be approved in a combat kit. There is a special combat kit for every piece of artillery. Here it says that since mortars are weapons that use indirect fire rather than direct fire, their degree of precision is very low which needs and necessitates a correction of fire in order to reduce the consumption of ammunition to the best possible level.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 420 it says independent mortar squad, 82-millimetres, carries out group firing by targeting isolated firing points, groups of marksmen --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters didn't manage to translate everything before the next page was ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us about some -- the following paragraph in terms of the size of the space that is targeted by 82-millimetre mortars?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC
utterances.text: These are 120 to 150 square metres --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you start over again. Please put a pause.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand. But please forgive me. I simply get carried away by the question. An 82-millimetre mortar platoon targets the area 100 times 250 metres, and then below you can see that these targets are firing squad and defence, firing platoon in attack, and based on the data available I reached the figure of 2200 legitimate targets in Sarajevo and this is the basis that I used for computing it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. As for 421, you already explained what the systematic fire is and what the combination of firing --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speakers please pause between questions and answers. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. The interpreters even didn't finish your question, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry. Mainly they managed to finish the combination of two, which means systematic fire and the combination thereof. The General said "concentrated" and that's how I would like to have it interpreted.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What are firing strikes and what is a systematic fire? You said "concentrated fire"?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC
utterances.text: Fire strikes means that several weapons are engaging the same target at the same time, which means that it's a concentrated fire targeting one and the same target.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We heard testimony here of a foreign observer. I asked him how he knew that it was random fire and he replied by saying, "Well, if it's concentrated fire, it's not random; but when you have isolated fire, it's not random fire." What would you say to that?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC
utterances.text: I wouldn't agree with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I would like to have the reference.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Regretfully, I'm not able to give you the reference now. I can do it through re-direct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: 423 speaks about systematic fire and 424 speaks about the combination. When is this method applied, the combination?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC
utterances.text: It is being applied when you have to sustain the regime of fire which keeps the enemy constantly in fear of being exposed to strikes. Occasionally you can combine it with the devastating strike which adds to the seriousness of the activity.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have the next page.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 425, what does it specify? Can you tell us something about it?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC
utterances.text: These are different types of fire applied by fire platoons for neutralisation, destruction, and blinding. So these are the different types of fire. Artillerymen know that better. I'm not an artilleryman myself. So it's not exactly my speciality, but as a military officer I know this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In terms of types of fire and without being aware of the objective or purpose, actually, can one conclude that a particular fire is non-selective or unprofessional?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC
utterances.text: No, not on that basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you focus on these tables now? Can you tell us what they prescribe?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC
utterances.text: They prescribe what I already referred to, how many projectiles have to be fired in order to reach a degree of neutralisation, degree of neutralisation of the objective 15 to 25 per cent, 15 then number of shells per company, 24, how many projectiles are fired at personnel.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I see. The one down here, 15 to 25, 12 shells per hectare, what does that mean? Does it mean that it is customary that in order to neutralise an objective, an average of 12 shells have to be fired?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but in order to neutralise only 15 to 25 per cent.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What about 40 to 50 per cent?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC
utterances.text: 50 to 40 per cent, 48, that would be the number of shells per hectare.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could these pages please be added to the number that we had?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. While it's -- it would not be that critical, could you take a look at footnote 190. The second item in that footnote refers to a 120-millimetre mortar rules which was allegedly published by the JNA General Staff, but the year was noted as 2001, if you could take a look. Probably the General can assist us since it is his report. In the meantime, let us continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Your Excellency, that is precisely why I called up only this rule that was published in 1982. I didn't even make an effort to find this one from 2001.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC
utterances.text: I took both into account.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: My question is now a JNA -- yes, how could JNA publish this in 2001? Whether JNA existed in 2001?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, it's not the JNA, it's the VJ, the Army of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Maybe it's wrong in the translation. In the original it says "VJ."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. In the English version it said "JNA," yes. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, sir, in paragraphs 300 onwards you dealt with the use of snipers in the Sarajevo theatre of war. What is your conclusion in relation to the use of snipers and what is being asserted in respect of that use of fire?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC
utterances.text: If I were to try to answer this question more succinctly, and it's a rather broad question, this is what I would say: I dealt with sniping here as part of the content of combat activities. Sniping is a legitimate military activity, legitimate. Snipers and sniping were used by both sides. However, the 1st Corps of the BH Army had a significant advantage in relation to the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps as far as that part of military power was concerned. Why? Because they had more favourable positions for sniping; that is to say, they were on elevations around the city, then also within the city, built-up areas, high-rises that were often used for sniping. Also, the 1st Corps had a larger number of snipers as such, because when the war started the factory Zrak, which did manufacture this optical equipment for snipers for this kind of weaponry -- well, all of this was distributed to units of the 1st Corps of the BH. Then the 1st Corps of the BH Army had 12.7-millimetre snipers from the very beginning of the war, whereas the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps got this weaponry only in 1994. And - which is even more important - the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps did not have any sniper units. I mean in all the documents that I managed to study -- well, it was only in one document of the Ilijas Brigade that I came across this information, that they had a unit consisting of nine sharpshooters. Not in any other unit of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps did I find that. As for the units of the 1st Corps of the BH Army, I came across lots of information to the effect that each brigade had a sniper unit of their own.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: "Unit" is the interpretation that was unit here in -- on this page. Would that be "platoon"?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: The word is "squad."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Three squads make up a platoon. Now, these nine men, that unit, they comprised a squad.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now it has been corrected and I thank the interpreters for that. Can you tell us where this Ilijas Brigade was oriented, this brigade that had that squad of sharpshooters, were they facing the city or were they facing the external area?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We did not manage to follow the answer because we were still interpreting the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you kindly repeat your answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When I answered questions related to the Sarajevo theatre of war, I referred to Ilijas and that's the place where this brigade is from. I placed it in this broader aspect of the Sarajevo theatre of war, that is to say outside the urban areas. That is a settlement that is about 10 kilometres out of town. So this brigade with that squad was not oriented towards town.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. General, sir, finally, can you tell us what it was that you concluded about command responsibility and the role and participation of the president of the republic in active military combat in relation to Srebrenica and after Srebrenica? Your Chapter 2.3 deals with that.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I looked at Operation Krivaja 95 in the context of your powers in terms of control, and as far as launching the operation is concerned and its development and its outcome, you did not have direct responsibility; that is, exclusively within the responsibility of the Main Staff, or rather, the command of the Drina Corps. You did receive reports about how the operation developed. However, as for direct involvement in this operation except for the 9th when you agreed that they entered town, I did not come across a single document that directly pertained to that operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is that strange? What is the role otherwise at strategic level of command in operative and tactical actions?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC
utterances.text: This is nothing strange. Because operative command was under the Main Staff, you did not deal with that. Otherwise, an operation at that level is exclusively under the corps commander and he seeks the approval of the commander of the Main Staff, not the approval of yourself; however, since this was not a strategic operation, that's why this was not indispensable. And secondly, you would have interfered only if the forces had been used in an illegal way and for illegitimate objectives. Since that had not been the case, you did not interfere. From the reports you did not have any indications --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters did not hear the end of the sentence. Could the witness please speak into the microphone. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you repeat your last sentence. From the report, you did not have any indications. From there, Mr. Radinovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand. In the reports that you received from the ground, from the Main Staff, there were no reasons -- there were no reasons for you to intervene or for you to issue any kind of corrective orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Your report also deals with legitimacy of military operations since these two zones had not been demilitarised. What is the obligation of the parties involved in demilitarisation if one of the parties violates it, not to say constantly violates the main provisions of the agreement? Were we duty-bound to continue to consider those zones to be demilitarised if they had not been demilitarised?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC
utterances.text: You did not have the obligation to behave towards these zones as demilitarised zones if they had not been demilitarised and they indeed had not been. The obligation of the other side was to demilitarise them in accordance with the agreement reached in May 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you familiarise yourself with documents from April 1993 when the counter-offensive of the Army of Republika Srpska towards Srebrenica was stopped?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. When the Army of Republika Srpska intended to enter Srebrenica in April of 1993, they were stopped on your explicit orders, not to enter. As a matter of fact, you even did not want investigations to be carried out in this very heated atmosphere so that no mistakes would be made.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you notice in this preparatory order vis-a-vis Srebrenica what was the actual task involved? What were the intentions involved, and when was there a change in the plan?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC
utterances.text: The preparatory order for carrying out Krivaja 95 was issued on the 2nd of July, 1995, and the order for carrying it out was issued on the 4th, that is to say within two days. As regards the objective of that operation there is no significant difference. The objective was the physical separation of the enclaves, the physical separation of the enclaves; controlling the area between the enclaves in order to prevent misusing that area by the 28th Division so that they could not operate against the civilians there, the Serb civilians. And the reports of the 28th Division from the 28th and 30th of June show that they are reporting to the 2nd Corps in Tuzla, saying that they had sabotage groups there and that they killed 40 Chetniks. Others say that there were even 70 of them, and they say that they seized lots of weapons and cattle.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us how this happened, or rather, more specifically --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, I just want to clarify something here on the record, page 91, lines 7 and 8 and 9. I'm just wondering whether there was a mistake in translation or whether the General misspoke because it says here 2nd of July and 4th of July. Is that a translation error? Did you misspeak, General? It should be the same date.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe it is a mistake because it's the 2nd of July, but there are some brigade ones from the 4th of July, so then perhaps there may have been some confusion there.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There are two documents. One is the preparatory order and the other one is the order --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The question is about the date of those two documents.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. The preparatory order was certainly on the 2nd, and the order -- now, this moment I cannot say. I think it was on the 2nd of July, but the operation started on the 6th, or rather, the 7th.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: How did you assess my consent, or rather, agreement to changing the plan in view of the reports that conditions had been created for the army to enter? Was this justified from a military point of view and did that have anything to do with the situation in Srebrenica itself and the departure of the 28th Division, or rather, their readiness to leave?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC
utterances.text: There is yet another example which demonstrate what your role was and how it was understood by military commanders. For as long as the course of the operation was aiming at separating the enclaves, which was the principal and primary objective defined in the relevant order, there was no need to ask for your approval. Once a need arose for the army to enter the town which profoundly changed the situation, then your approval was required. And they did seek your approval to enter the town. Since the town was starting to be vacated, there was a possibility of an army resistance and possibility of disturbing the balance and some undesirable occurrences, and therefore you gave your approval for them to enter the town but you explicitly said that protection must be provided for the civilians --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can the witness please finish the sentence. We couldn't hear what he said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you repeat your last sentence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In response to this question I underlined the fact that entering the town constituted a substantial change of the objectives of the operation which required an approval from the Commander-in-Chief, and he did give his approval to the command who was in charge of the operation and he conveyed this consent through General Tolimir to the forward command post of the Drina Corps. In other words, the Commander-in-Chief gave his approval for them to enter the town but that they must observe the rules of international law with regard to the civilian population.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In the consent that I gave, was there any reference made to prisoners of war?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. It was said that everybody who took part in combat should be afforded the status of prisoners of war.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Based on the documents, were you able to see how the capturing of prisoners took place throughout the conflict and whether this procedure of capturing was carried out in accordance with the law of -- customary law? I'm talking in general.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC
utterances.text: Generally speaking, this involved capturing troops who were in the process of breaking through, and column was acting against forces that were setting ambushes along the route of their breakthrough. Therefore, it was completely legitimate to act against them, including to capture those who were in the column and engaged in certain activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Have you concluded that there was something unusual or illicit or alarming in the process of taking prisoners and gathering them at one point, transporting them, or putting them up at a certain location? Was anything done that would be either alarming or unusual?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC
utterances.text: I did not detect anything in the documents that would cause alarm and that would require your intervention.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. During the war we had a witness who said that there were over 20.000 prisoners. Did you come across any document that speaks about illegal executions and about my role in particular in that respect during the war? And then we'll move on to Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic should by now know that he has to give a reference when he claims that a certain witness said something, and I find it a bit unfair that he doesn't do it. It's not so helpful for us to get it in the re-direct. We need to have the reference now.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. I withdraw this information.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, in the documents or in any other way, did you manage to find out what kind of orders I issued and what my role was in the events that followed the liberation of Srebrenica, particularly with regard to prisoners of war?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC
utterances.text: On the 11th of July when the Army of Republika Srpska entered Srebrenica, you appointed a civilian commissioner by issuing an order to that respect and you also ordered a police station to be set up in order to carry out control. You prohibited any form of unlawful treatment of civilians. You insisted on those who were engaged in fighting against the VRS to be given the status of prisoners of war, and you expressed, generally speaking, an acceptable attitude towards civilians. At the time when you issued these documents, you were obviously expecting the civilians to remain in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. According to what you have studied, can you accept the assertion that the population in question was forcibly deported from Srebrenica against their own will and with the use of force? I'm talking about military actions that were taken, do they indicate that this constituted a forcible relocation? What was your conclusion --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Yes, please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not find any piece of information that would indicate that any actions were taken that would justify this assertion that this was a forcible expulsion. I primarily referred to an array of information and facts that are contained in documents. I'm referring to a document dated the 9th of July, whereby the civilian authorities of Srebrenica asked the leadership of Bosnia-Herzegovina for the Srebrenica population to be moved out of Srebrenica because the 28th Division was not defending the town.
